What this metric tells us is that across the 34,836 studied wildlife populations, the average decline was 73%.
facts.measure: monitored populations (Living Planet Index: average relative change in vertebrate population size)
facts.unit: % average decline in population size
facts.notes: Population sizes of monitored vertebrate populations, averaged (geometric mean of rates of change); not biomass, not a species count, not extinctions. About half the populations declined and half rose or held steady (same page). Our World in Data's guide to the WWF Living Planet Report 2024 (WWF's own pages refuse the downloader); OWID marks it outdated since the 2026 report (ext-present-lpi-2026).

check.reason: Both quotes verbatim (OWID, 10 Oct 2024). 73% average decline in monitored population size across 34,836 populations, 1970-2020; not a loss of individuals or species. The LPI tracks vertebrate populations, as the IPBES SPM also states. OWID notes the 2024 and 2026 indexes are recalculated, not a time series.

facts.claim: The 2026 Living Planet Index reports that studied wildlife populations of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish declined by an average of 73% from 1970 through 2022, across 35,803 studied populations.
quotes: The headline figure from the 2026 update of the LPI is that studied wildlife populations declined by an average of 73% from 1970 through 2022.
This covers mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish; it doesn't yet include invertebrates or plants.
Across the 35,803 wildlife populations studied, the average decline was 73%.
facts.measure: monitored populations (Living Planet Index: average relative change in vertebrate population size)
facts.unit: % average decline in population size
facts.notes: The latest edition (report published 8 October 2026). Vertebrate population sizes only, no invertebrates or plants; not biomass. Same 73% as the 2024 edition but over a longer span and more populations; the whole trend line shifts with each edition's data. Our World in Data's overview of the WWF Living Planet Report 2026.

check.reason: All three quotes verbatim (OWID, Ritchie, 8 Oct 2026). 73% average decline across 35,803 vertebrate populations, 1970-2022. It is the same 73% as 2024 over a longer span because the whole index was recomputed, so do not plot the two editions as a trend.

facts.claim: Human activity contributed to the Quaternary Megafauna Extinction between about 50,000 and 3,000 years ago, which claimed around half of the large (over 40 kg) land mammal species (Bar-On et al. 2018).
quotes: Human activity contributed to the Quaternary Megafauna Extinction between ≈50,000 and ≈3,000 y ago, which claimed around half of the large (>40 kg) land mammal species ( 30 ).
facts.measure: date (span of the late Pleistocene megafaunal extinction); around half of large land mammal species lost
facts.unit: years ago (start of the span; end ≈3,000 years ago)
facts.notes: Megafauna threshold here is >40 kg (Barnosky 2008 uses >44 kg, Wikipedia 45 kg). Europe PMC full text of Bar-On, Phillips and Milo 2018, PNAS.

check.reason: Quote verbatim; the 50,000-3,000 years ago span matches the cited Barnosky 2008 abstract. The claim's threshold needs correcting: the main text says >40 kg, but the paper's own SI (over 100 lb, i.e. 44 kg) and its cited source both say >44 kg. The SI dates the extinction 50,000-7,000 years ago.

facts.claim: The Quaternary Megafauna Extinction claimed two-thirds of mammal genera and one-half of species weighing more than 44 kg, between approximately 50,000 and 3,000 years ago (Barnosky 2008).
quotes: Earth's most recent major extinction episode, the Quaternary Megafauna Extinction, claimed two-thirds of mammal genera and one-half of species that weighed >44 kg between approximately 50,000 and 3,000 years ago.
facts.measure: genera lost (megafaunal mammal genera over 44 kg; also one-half of such species) and the span
facts.unit: % of mammal genera weighing >44 kg (two-thirds); one-half of such species
facts.notes: Large mammals only (>44 kg). PubMed abstract (NCBI E-utilities, plain text) of Barnosky AD (2008) 'Megafauna biomass tradeoff as a driver of Quaternary and future extinctions', PNAS 105 Suppl 1:11543-11548, doi:10.1073/pnas.0801918105.

check.reason: Quote verbatim in the PubMed abstract (PNAS 105 Suppl 1:11543, Aug 2008). The >44 kg threshold applies to both counts: two-thirds (66.7%) of megafaunal mammal genera and half of megafaunal species, about 50,000-3,000 years ago.

facts.claim: Growth of human biomass largely matched the loss of non-human megafauna biomass until about 12,000 years ago, when total megafauna biomass crashed; pre-crash biomass levels, now concentrated in humans, were regained just before the Industrial Revolution and then rose far above the pre-crash baseline with fossil fuels (Barnosky 2008).
quotes: Estimates of megafauna biomass (including humans as a megafauna species) for before, during, and after the extinction episode suggest that growth of human biomass largely matched the loss of non-human megafauna biomass until approximately 12,000 years ago. Then, total megafauna biomass crashed, because many non-human megafauna species suddenly disappeared, whereas human biomass continued to rise.

Precrash biomass levels were finally reached just before the Industrial Revolution began, then skyrocketed above the precrash baseline as humans augmented the energy available to the global ecosystem by mining fossil fuels.
facts.measure: date (crash and recovery of megafauna biomass, humans included)
facts.unit: years ago (crash of total megafauna biomass)
facts.when: crash ≈12,000 years ago; pre-crash level regained just before the Industrial Revolution
facts.notes: The rebound is of megafauna biomass INCLUDING humans (after the crash concentrated in one species, humans), not a recovery of wild animals: wild mammal biomass remains ≈6-fold below its prehuman level (ext-present-wild-mammal-biomass-total-baron). PubMed abstract of Barnosky 2008, PNAS.

check.reason: Both quotes verbatim in the abstract. The measure is total megafauna biomass with humans counted as megafauna: it crashed after about 12,000 years ago and regained the pre-crash level just before the Industrial Revolution. Label the rebound as human biomass, not wild diversity.

facts.claim: Major late Pleistocene megafaunal extinctions occurred in Sahul (Australia-New Guinea) beginning around 50,000 years ago and in the Americas about 13,000 years ago, while extinctions in northern Eurasia were staggered between 50,000 and 10,000 years ago.
quotes: Major extinctions occurred in Australia-New Guinea (Sahul) beginning around 50,000 years ago and in the Americas about 13,000 years ago, coinciding in time with the migration of modern humans into these regions.
Extinctions in northern Eurasia were staggered over tens of thousands of years between 50,000 and 10,000 years ago
facts.measure: date (regional timing of the late Pleistocene megafaunal extinctions)
facts.unit: years ago (start, Sahul; Americas ≈13,000; northern Eurasia 50,000-10,000)
facts.notes: The same lead says extinctions in the Americas spanned only 3,000 years at most. Wikipedia, Late Pleistocene extinctions (lead).

check.reason: Both quotes verbatim in the lead: Sahul from about 50,000 years ago, the Americas about 13,000 (within at most 3,000 years), northern Eurasia staggered 50,000-10,000. Barnosky et al. 2004 (the article's ref. 13) also has the megafaunal genera gone between 50,000 and 10,000 years ago.

facts.claim: Megafauna are typically defined as animal species of 45 kg or more; during the Late Pleistocene about 65% of all megafaunal species worldwide became extinct, rising to 72% in North America, 83% in South America and 88% in Australia.
quotes: which are typically defined as animal species having body masses of 45 kg (99 lb) or more
Overall, during the Late Pleistocene about 65% of all megafaunal species worldwide became extinct,[12] rising to 72% in North America, 83% in South America and 88% in Australia
facts.measure: megafaunal species lost (animals of 45 kg or more)
facts.unit: % of megafaunal species worldwide (North America 72%, South America 83%, Australia 88%)
facts.notes: Large animals only; a species count, not biomass. Wikipedia, Late Pleistocene extinctions (lead).

check.reason: Quotes verbatim, but Wikipedia labels genus counts as species. Its ref. 12 (Saltré et al. 2016, PMC4740174) opens with about 65% of megafauna genera (>40 kg) lost in the late Quaternary. Its ref. 13 (Barnosky et al. 2004, Science 306:70, Table 1, faculty.washington.edu/stevehar/BarnoskyEtAl2004.pdf) gives 72/83/88% as the percent of mammalian megafaunal genera lost per continent. At species level, the primary papers in this set give about half (Barnosky 2008; Bar-On 2018).

facts.claim: The International Commission on Stratigraphy defines the Holocene, the current epoch, as starting approximately 11,700 years before 2000 CE (9,700 BCE).
quotes: The International Commission on Stratigraphy has defined the Holocene as starting approximately 11,700 years before 2000 CE (11,650 cal years BP, or 9,700 BCE).
facts.measure: date (start of the Holocene epoch, in which the present extinction is named)
facts.unit: years before 2000 CE
facts.notes: The epoch, not the extinction: Wikipedia's Holocene extinction article says the event's start is debated, with no consensus on when it began or whether it is distinct from the Quaternary (late Pleistocene) extinctions. Wikipedia, Holocene.

check.reason: Quote verbatim in Wikipedia's Holocene article: the ICS definition is about 11,700 years before 2000 CE (11,650 cal BP, 9,700 BCE). Date, unit and span right.
